title: Ontarians' Perceptions of Public Health Communications and Misinformation During the COVID-19 Pandemic: Survey Study
screen_reason: Web-based survey of 1,823 Ontario residents (June-December 2020) reporting the share of respondents who believed they had encountered COVID-19 misinformation: 55% (n=1010) 'sometimes, a lot, or quite a lot'. That is a self-reported exposure share with a population denominator, i.e. RECALL. Trust, source-use and information-difficulty items are not misinformation exposure and yield no rows.

estimates.platform: not platform-specific (self-reported encounters with COVID-19 misinformation in general)
estimates.measure_type: % of survey respondents who believed they encountered COVID-19 misinformation 'sometimes, a lot, or quite a lot'
estimates.denominator: 1,823 adult (>=18) residents of Ontario, Canada who participated in the web-based survey (convenience sample recruited via the Canadian Viewpoint market-research panel plus ads on the team's websites, Twitter, LinkedIn, Kijiji and Reddit)
estimates.definition: Respondent selected 'sometimes', 'a lot' or 'quite a lot' (rather than the lower categories) on the item asking how much COVID-19 misinformation they believed they had encountered
estimates.misinfo_def: "Although misinformation and disinformation both involve the spread of false information, disinformation is false information that is purposefully disseminated to cause harm or serve a specific person, group, organization, or country agenda" (no definition was supplied to respondents; the survey measured perceptions)
estimates.source_quote: Of the study sample, 55% (n=1010) believed that they encountered misinformation “sometimes, a lot, or quite a lot.”
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Perceptions of Misinformation', p. 8 (also Abstract and Conclusions)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Pure self-report: respondents judged their own exposure on a 5-point Likert item collapsed into three categories; the authors state explicitly that they did not verify these perceptions ('we did not evaluate the quality of information that participants obtained and trusted'). Survey piloted for face validity; CHERRIES-compliant reporting; no response rate obtainable (open survey).
estimates.moderator_quote: We recruited a convenience sample of residents from Ontario, Canada. ... Data were collected between June 10, 2020, and December 31, 2020. ... The 5-point Likert response questions regarding agreement were grouped into 3 categories (eg, "strongly disagree and disagree," "neither agree/disagree," and "agree and strongly agree")
estimates.notes: denom_scope=population per the survey rule (the denominator is who was asked, 1,823 respondents, not a topic corpus). The threshold is 'sometimes, a lot, or quite a lot', i.e. a share above a frequency threshold rather than 'any exposure', so this is a mid-strictness recall estimate and is not directly comparable with 'ever encountered' items. breadth=false: respondents were asked about 'misinformation' with no definition supplied, so the veracity strictness is the respondent's own. The exact survey wording is in Multimedia Appendix 1, which is not part of this text.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) 'Perceived drivers of misinformation' (social media/community influencers 1258, 69%; news media 967, 53%; international 735, 40%; federal 674, 37%; provincial 649, 35%; academia 537, 29%; other 328, 18%) were NOT extracted: they measure who respondents blame for misinformation, not whether they encountered any, and the instructions count only perceived amount/encounters. (2) Information-seeking difficulties ('difficulty determining the accuracy of information' 1053, 58%; sorting conflicting information 1061, 58%) are appraisal difficulty, not misinformation exposure. (3) Trust in sources (Table 3) and source use (Table 2) are not misinformation measures. (4) Gender and age ORs for reporting encountering misinformation (men OR 1.29, 95% CI 1.08-1.55; ages 41-60 OR 0.64; >=61 OR 0.36) are subgroup effect sizes, not shares, and the paper's headline is the pooled 55%, so no subgroup rows were created. (5) A minor internal inconsistency: the Discussion says 'Over 50% of respondents reported encountering COVID-19-related misinformation' while the Results give 55% (n=1010); the Results figure is used.

rob.design: Open web-based (Qualtrics) convenience survey of Ontario residents recruited through the Canadian Viewpoint panel email listservs plus website/Twitter/LinkedIn/Kijiji/Reddit ads; CHERRIES-compliant; 1,823 analysed after excluding duplicates, <5% completion and non-Ontario residents; no response rate reportable; questions not mandatory (item non-response of about 6% visible in Table 1); quantitative data summarised descriptively, ordinal regression for age/gender with a biostatistician overseeing; self-reported outcome never validated against content ('we did not assess the quality of information obtained and whether the participants' perceptions of misinformation correlated with data validity').
rob.item6_quote: Although misinformation and disinformation both involve the spread of false information, disinformation is false information that is purposefully disseminated to cause harm or serve a specific person, group, organization, or country agenda [3,4].
rob.item10_quote: Of the study sample, 55% (n=1010) believed that they encountered misinformation "sometimes, a lot, or quite a lot."
